highlightAliases.old: Clozapine 6.25–75 mg/day — low EPS risk, so a good option for psychotic symptoms in DLB (DLB/PD patients are extremely EPS-sensitive, except to clozapine); limited by neutropenia/agranulocytosis — weekly blood draws in the first 6 months (p928).
highlightAliases.new: Clozapine 6.25–75 mg/day — lower motor risk than potent dopamine blockers, but it can still cause serious harm. Evidence of benefit comes from Parkinson disease psychosis. Efficacy and tolerability specifically in DLB remain uncertain. Seek specialist input if persistent dangerous or severely distressing psychosis warrants a trial. DLB Consortium consensus. Use is limited by neutropenia/agranulocytosis — weekly blood draws in the first 6 months (p928).

highlightAliases.new: Mirtazapine — sedating at lower doses; in the sleep pilot, 8 received mirtazapine and 16 placebo (24 total). Nighttime sleep did not improve and daytime sleepiness increased. Page 930 misstates the treatment-group size. Scoralick et al., methods and results.

highlightAliases.old: Clozapine — limited by serious adverse effects (neutropenia/agranulocytosis) and close laboratory monitoring: weekly blood draws in the first 6 months (p928).
highlightAliases.new: Clozapine has lower motor toxicity, but efficacy and tolerability in dementia with Lewy bodies are uncertain. Neutropenia can be life-threatening and requires absolute neutrophil count monitoring, typically weekly in the first six months (p928).
